overview: The Aaniiih, also called Gros Ventre, are an Algonquian-speaking northern Plains people. The map’s Aaniiih record from 1530 to 1650 and Gros Ventre record from 1650 to 1783 use the same outline in northern Montana and southern Canada. These are coverage intervals, not separate peoples or lifetimes. At Fort Belknap, Aaniiih people share government with the distinct Nakoda nation.

periods.title: A large recognised territory
periods.summary: The 1855 treaty designated a large territory north of the Missouri and Musselshell rivers for the Blackfeet Nation, including the Gros Ventre.

periods.title: Fort Belknap is established
periods.summary: In 1888, the larger reserve was divided into smaller reservations, including Fort Belknap for Gros Ventre and Assiniboine people.

periods.title: A further reduction of the land base
periods.summary: Further land was ceded along Fort Belknap’s southern boundary in 1895, reducing the territory available to the communities living there.

periods.title: Building a tribal college
periods.summary: The Fort Belknap Indian Community chartered its college in November 1983 to meet local educational needs and support cultural renewal. It became a lasting community institution.

periods.title: Teaching a new generation of speakers
periods.summary: White Clay Immersion School opened in 2003 within the tribal college. Children learned through Aaniiih throughout the school day, extending language renewal into formal education.

items.text: An encounter recorded around 1754 placed Aaniiih people near the Saskatchewan River’s forks. Later alliances connected them with the Blackfeet: their history extends across today’s national border.
In 1876, Aaniiih people refused an agency move toward hostile neighbors, sacrificing annuities. Fort Belknap reopened in 1878. Refusal was a way to resist federal relocation.

The community’s history describes buffalo as a source of food, clothing and tipi coverings. Following herds required knowledge of animal movement and the skills to preserve meat and work hides for several different purposes.

In testimony gathered in 1901, women described slicing meat thinly and drying it on racks. Dried meat could be stored in rawhide containers or pounded with berries. Preservation supported households beyond the immediate hunt.

Tent making could be cooperative: a woman with enough prepared hides invited skilled makers to a feast. An expert fitted the pieces before others sewed them together, combining hospitality with specialised work.

Kroeber described a child’s robe, museum number 50-1751, decorated with coloured quillwork, tin and dyed horsehair pendants. The object records several materials and techniques used together in clothing.
A soft-hide bag, museum number 50-1738, appears in the same report. Such bags carried clothing and small household articles, with quillwork and beadwork adding decoration to a practical container.

Aaniiih Nakoda College was designed to make further education available near home and reflect the lifeways of both Nations. Its programmes connect cultural study with fields such as ecology, nursing, computing and trades. The name adopted in 2011 explicitly recognises both peoples.

In 2014, educator Clarena Brockie described White Clay Immersion School’s use of community projects, field learning and teaching between generations. Language was the means of learning across subjects, giving children sustained opportunities to use it.

A reference grammar published in 2024 grew from work by Andrew Cowell, Terry Brockie and tribal members to retranscribe archival language records. It explains both earlier and modern forms, supporting community decisions about what to teach and how.

The grammar also treats place names, personal names, greetings and traditional narrative. Preserving language involves how people address one another and describe their world, alongside its sounds and word structures.

sections.title: Buffalo and the work of restoration

items.text: In August 2013, Yellowstone-origin bison arrived from Fort Peck to establish a new cultural herd at Fort Belknap. The project linked conservation with food and ceremonial uses. This was a specific restoration programme within an already living community.

A project funded in 2024 planned wildlife-friendly fencing and a livestock water system to bring more pasture into the buffalo grazing system. Managing a herd also involves water, land access, infrastructure and consultation about cultural resources.

sections.title: Games, written words and new community work

items.text: A Montana teaching resource reproduces a historic Gros Ventre shinny ball and curved stick. The ball’s buckskin covering was sewn around buffalo-hair stuffing. It is a useful reminder that a ball does not have to come from a factory: players and makers could turn available materials into sporting equipment.

In 1999, Aaniiih artist Chandler Good Strike made a model parfleche case now in the National Museum of the American Indian. He folded, painted and tied rawhide, adding felt and synthetic fabric. This documented modern work carries a container-making tradition forward through the materials and choices of an individual artist.

A short written sample is “báyaaah,” translated “house, home” in the 2012 Gros Ventre/White Clay Student Dictionary. Andrew Cowell compiled it with Terry Brockie and John Stiff Arm, drawing on earlier work with speakers. This is an attested modern teaching spelling, not a reconstructed inscription from 1650.

A 2012 library grant proposed putting Aaniiih and Nakoda translations into popular children’s books. After requesting publishers’ permission, staff would print translations on transparent labels and attach them to the pages. Familiar pictures could then accompany community languages during reading sessions and at local libraries.

A 2021 account describes college students trapping mosquitoes and testing them for West Nile virus. Samples also went to another laboratory for quality checks. This is a modern form of community health work in which students investigate the insects around their own homes and help provide information for public alerts.

The same college account describes a long-term study of organisms in the Milk River, a local drinking-water source. Studying the river’s living community adds evidence about water conditions. Classroom science becomes closely connected to an everyday question: what is happening in the water people depend on?

Fort Belknap began returning buffalo in the late 1970s, according to its buffalo program’s contribution to a 2022 Smithsonian research announcement. The shared community program connects ecological restoration with food and cultural relationships. Buffalo therefore belong in this story’s future as well as in its account of historic hunting.

ending.text: Reservation confinement and assimilation policies reduced Aaniiih autonomy and disrupted language transmission. Aaniiih people continue, sharing the Fort Belknap government with Nakoda neighbours and building institutions for education and cultural renewal. The decline of fluent speakers did not mean the disappearance of the people or an end to language learning.
